hook: Why your $16 sconce won't light your hallway

scenes.visual_prompt: Slow pan across a dark hallway floor at night, barely visible
scenes.on_screen_text: Dark hallway. 11pm. You know this walk.
scenes.voiceover: You know this walk — down a dark hallway, feeling for the wall.

scenes.visual_prompt: Plug-in sconce glowing on the wall, camera tilts down to show floor still unlit
scenes.on_screen_text: The $16 sconce lights THIS. Not this.
scenes.voiceover: A plug-in sconce lights the wall it's plugged into. It doesn't touch the floor.

scenes.visual_prompt: Product shot of a 2-pack motion sensor light, $11.99 price tag overlay
scenes.voiceover: For $11.99, you get two motion-sensor lights instead — one for the hallway, one for a closet or bathroom.

scenes.visual_prompt: Demo: foot steps near outlet, light triggers instantly, cool white glow along baseboard
scenes.on_screen_text: No switch. No reaching in the dark.
scenes.voiceover: They trigger the second you walk past — no switch, no fumbling.

scenes.visual_prompt: Side-by-side: warm sconce up high, cool motion light down low, both on in same hallway
scenes.on_screen_text: Warm light up top. Safety light down low.
scenes.voiceover: Keep the warm sconce for ambiance up top, and let the motion light handle the actual walking.

scenes.visual_prompt: Text card reading 'Category fact: reviewers say the same thing repeatedly'
scenes.on_screen_text: Not a guess. It's the pattern in the reviews.
scenes.voiceover: This isn't one opinion — it's the pattern that shows up across dozens of reviews in this category.

caption: The $16 plug-in sconce trend is real, but review threads keep pointing at the same gap: it lights a wall, not a path. Here's the $11.99 fix. Blog post has the full spec breakdown — link in bio.
